Earlier than 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice had already filed a lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of having a "smartphone monopoly".

Over the past two years, Apple has repeatedly publicly expressed opposition to this case. According to the latest report by Bloomberg, the Department of Justice and Apple are currently in negotiations to settle the lawsuit.

The Bloomberg report said that Apple has made "multiple offers" so far this year, attempting to reach a settlement with the Department of Justice:

The report also reminded that although the negotiations are still ongoing, there is no guarantee that Apple and the Department of Justice will ultimately reach an agreement.

The Department of Justice's antitrust lawsuit against Apple revolves around five major areas of the iPhone experience: super apps, cloud streaming games, third-party instant messaging apps, third-party smartwatches, and third-party digital wallets.

Apple has made a number of substantive changes over the past year in response to the Department of Justice's concerns, including supporting the RCS communication standard in the "Messages" app, launching a new "Mini App Partner Program" in the App Store, and expanding access to the iPhone's NFC chip.

Whether these changes can satisfy the Department of Justice remains to be seen. As Bloomberg stated, political factors are also involved:

Apple and the Department of Justice have recently filed a joint status report on the latest progress of the case. In addition, Apple also won a document discovery dispute earlier this week, successfully preventing the Department of Justice from obtaining relevant documents from federal agencies.

9to5Mac Perspective

If Apple and the Department of Justice can ultimately reach a settlement, it will be a major burden lifted for John Ternus, who takes over as CEO in September.
